Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-07

Duration: 64 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jorge Alvarez (ML Infra Lead, DataFlux), Maya Chen (Platform Eng), Samir Patel (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Redwood team walked through JSON-mode and tool-calling performance characteristics. Customers asked about deterministic outputs for structured JSON, the extra tokens from constrained decoding, and how KV cache + batching interacts with repeated short calls. There was discussion of quantization artifacts on strict decoding, and how private deployments (VPC/on-prem) affect network latency and kernel selection. Next steps agreed: Redwood to run a constrained-decoding benchmark with DataFlux's sample prompts and share quantization checklist and perf scripts.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: we want to go deep on the json-mode tool-calling path, like how constrained decoding changes latency and throughput, plus kv-cache and batching interactions. Priya will do the runtime bits.
[00:00:18] Priya: Hi, yeah, thanks. first, quick note: when we talk about JSON mode here we mean the constrained decoding / structural constraints layer that enforces schema and reduces invalid outputs — that comes with a small decoding overhead depending on pattern complexity.
[00:00:36] Jorge: when you say overhead, are we talking per-token additional CPU on the host or more GPU stalls? where does it show up in p50 vs p95?
[00:00:48] Priya: good question. it's a mix. constrained decoding typically runs as a post-token filter that checks allowed tokens against schema state; for our runtime we optimize that by precomputing token-sets where possible and running the token-filter on the CPU in parallel with kernel execution. you see a small increase at p50 — like 5–12ms for short responses (under 64 tokens) — but p95/p99 can grow more if the model emits many ambiguous tokens requiring extra pruning. on A100-class hosts that's minimal; on quantized int8 paths or on CPU-forwarding setups the relative overhead is higher.
[00:01:22] Maya: ok, so for our use-case most calls are ~30 tokens response, and we do hundreds qps of single-turn tool calls. batching is important but we need low latency p50. what's the best practice?
[00:01:33] Priya: for single-turn short tool calls we recommend small-window batching with a very low wait threshold: like max batch size 8 and dispatch after 10–15ms idle. Combined with prefix caching (if many calls share identical prompts or system messages), you can avoid redoing the KV-state for the prefix. That greatly reduces per-call GPU compute.
[00:01:51] Samir: remind me how prefix/KV cache interacts with tool-calling where inputs vary a bit — we do templated prompts with variable fields.
[00:02:00] Priya: so the KV cache is keyed by the tokenized prefix. If your template is identical apart from slot values, we typically split the prompt: keep the stable instruction and system prefetched in the cache, and append the variable slot tokens at runtime. That way the heavy prefix compute is cached, only the tail runs per-request. For JSON-mode constrained decoding the schema state also resets per-call, so that part is per-request but it's cheap compared to full prefix recomputation.
[00:02:28] Jorge: is there any tension between batching and KV cache TTLs? Like if we scale up dedicated pools with autoscaling will caches be warmed appropriately?
[00:02:36] Alex: yes, autoscaling can evict caches — we support proactive warming via synthetic requests and sticky routing for critical routes. For Dedicated you can pin requests to a smaller pool to avoid cold caches, or use a warm-up worker set.
[00:02:50] Maya: quantization — we've been testing int8 to reduce cost. how does that affect deterministic JSON outputs? we care about exact field names and trailing commas — basically strict parseability.
[00:03:02] Priya: quantization has two axes: model numeric fidelity and decoding stability. For many models int8 (Q8) performs well for free-text, but small logits differences can make constrained decoding choose different tokens if multiple tokens are close in probability. That can manifest as extra whitespace or different punctuation. We recommend running an eval set with your strict JSON parser across quantized variants. For mission-critical structured outputs we often recommend BF16 or Q4_0 with per-layer calibration; we can share a recommended quantization profile.
[00:03:31] Samir: is there a config knob to bias toward fewer unpredictable tokens? like temperature or repetition penalties?
[00:03:38] Priya: yes, temperature/beam/penalties still apply. We also expose a "delta-safe-mode" which reduces sampling variance for constrained decoding (it narrows allowed token probability gaps by applying a tiny smoothing). It increases p50 by a few ms but it improves parse rates for strict JSON.
[00:03:56] Jorge: networking: since we run in a VPC with private deployment, how much network overhead is added when we host the model on-prem vs dedicated Redwood-hosted?
[00:04:06] Alex: for Private (VPC/on-prem) you remove the public hop, but you should account for intra-datacenter latency — the big difference is where the tokenization and pre/postprocessing run. If you host runtime local to your app, you get lower network latency but you take on NIC utilization and scheduling. For our Private package we provide profiling hooks and a recommended topology: colocate a light-weight tokenizer/sidecar near app nodes, and route inference RPCs to the nearest serving pool. We also provide perf scripts to measure RPC+decode roundtrip.
[00:04:38] Maya: could you share the perf scripts?
[00:04:40] Alex: yes — we'll share the github link. (link: https://redwood.dev/perf/json-mode-benchmarks) note: that's internal perf repo access, we will add DataFlux test vectors.
[00:04:50] Priya: back to batching: for tool-calls that call external tools we sometimes see tail latency from the external tool dominating. Redwood supports streaming partial tokens so you can start downstream tool invocation earlier, but for strict JSON you usually want complete structured output before calling other services. one trick is to stream and run a local parse-check to abort early if invalid, else wait for full output.
[00:05:16] Jorge: do you have numbers for token-per-second improvements when using prefix caching vs cold runs?
[00:05:23] Priya: in our tests with 2k-token prefixes and 32-token responses, a warmed KV cache can reduce end-to-end GPU time by ~60–75%, mostly by avoiding recomputation of the prefix layers. For short prompts the absolute improvement is smaller but still material because it avoids repeated memory copies into GPU and reduces kernel launches.
[00:05:45] Samir: we also care about scaling cost — do you support mixed-precision per-model? like run the first layers fp16 and final layers int8?
[00:05:53] Priya: our runtime can do per-layer quantization profiles — it's not trivial but we do calibrated hybrid profiles. That is part of the Optimize feature set; for a POC we can recommend a profile that balances quality and tokens-per-second.
[00:06:06] Maya: security/compliance question: in VPC deployment, where are logs and structured outputs stored? we need audit trail but also limited retention.
[00:06:14] Alex: for Private you control log retention. We ship audit hooks that emit redacted transcripts to your S3/Blob with customer-managed KMS. For Dedicated/Hosted we offer retention tiers and SOC2-compatible export pipelines.
[00:06:26] Jorge: practical POC — what do you need from us to run the constrained-decoding benchmark that matches our workload?
[00:06:32] Priya: a few things: 1) representative prompt set (templates plus slot variations), 2) expected JSON schemas / grammar, 3) sample QPS and typical response len, 4) your preferred quantization profiles to test (if any), and 5) whether you'll run Private or Dedicated. ideally we also get a small set of parse-fail examples.
[00:06:55] Jorge: we can provide those. we'll also include our strict JSON parser for pass/fail metrics.
[00:07:01] Alex: great. i'll summarize next steps.
[00:07:05] Priya: one more note: when you do strict schema enforcement we recommend attaching a short canonicalization pass — normalize whitespace and key order — that reduces false negatives from minor tokenization differences. it's cheap and helps parse rates on quantized models.
[00:07:20] Maya: can you send the delta-safe-mode perf tradeoff chart?
[00:07:23] Alex: yes — we'll include that in the follow-up.
[00:07:27] Samir: final Q: do you support running token-level constraints via an on-GPU implementation? to avoid CPU<->GPU sync?
[00:07:35] Priya: we have an experimental on-GPU constraints path for some model sizes; it reduces CPU overhead but increases kernel complexity. for production at scale today we rely on hybrid CPU-side token filtering because it's simpler and more flexible. we can discuss trying the GPU path in the POC if performance requires.
[00:07:54] Alex: ok, thanks everyone. quick recap of next steps and owners.
